questions.model_answer: Supervised learning uses labeled training data (input + correct output). The model learns from this labeled data and predicts outputs for new, unseen data. Examples include email spam classification (spam or not spam) and regression for salary prediction. Unsupervised learning uses unlabeled data (input only, no correct output). The model finds patterns, structure, clusters, or relationships automatically. Examples include customer segmentation and recommendation systems. Reinforcement learning focuses on how agents learn to interact with an environment to maximize cumulative rewards. The model learns by trial and error using rewards and penalties, without labeled data. Examples include robot navigation, game AI, and skill acquisition.

questions.question_text: Using the dataset where Class is the input and Number of students is the output, explain how to calculate θ₀ and θ₁ and predict the number of students for Class 6.
questions.model_answer: The dataset is: Class X = [1, 3, 5, 7, 8], Number of students Y = [10, 13, 14, 17, 19]. Compute Σx = 24, Σy = 73, Σxy = 390, Σx² = 148, n = 5. θ₁ = (nΣxy - ΣxΣy) / (nΣx² - (Σx)²) = (5×390 - 24×73) / (5×148 - 24²) = (1950 - 1752) / (740 - 576) = 198 / 164 ≈ 1.2. θ₀ = (ΣyΣx² - ΣxΣxy) / (nΣx² - (Σx)²) = (73×148 - 24×390) / 164 = (10804 - 9360) / 164 = 1444 / 164 ≈ 8.8. Hypothesis function: h(x) = 8.8 + 1.2x. For Class 6: h(6) = 8.8 + 1.2×6 = 8.8 + 7.2 = 16. So the predicted number of students is 16.

grading_rubric.description: Correctly computes Σx, Σy, Σxy, Σx², and n.
Correctly applies the formula and computes θ₁ ≈ 1.2.
Correctly applies the formula and computes θ₀ ≈ 8.8.
States h(x) = 8.8 + 1.2x.

questions.question_text: Explain the difference between binary, multi-class, and multi-label classification, and describe one strategy for adapting binary classifiers to multi-class problems.
questions.model_answer: Binary classification has only two possible outcomes (e.g., YES/NO, MALE/FEMALE, spam/not spam). Multi-class classification has more than two outcomes (e.g., classifying crops or careers), where each example belongs to exactly one class. Multi-label classification predicts 0 or more classes for each example, with no mutual exclusion (e.g., an image can contain a plane, boat, truck, and dog; a text document can have multiple topics). To adapt binary classifiers to multi-class problems, we can use one-versus-one or one-versus-rest approaches. One-versus-one trains as many classifiers as there are pairs of labels: for N labels, N×(N-1)/2 classifiers, with the final class predicted by majority vote. One-versus-rest trains N binary classifiers, each distinguishing one label from the rest.

questions.question_text: Compare eager learners and lazy learners in machine learning, giving at least two examples of each and explaining when each type is advantageous.
questions.model_answer: Eager learners are machine learning algorithms that first build a model from the training dataset before making any prediction on future datasets. They spend more time during training to achieve better generalization, but require less time to make predictions. Examples include Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine, Decision Trees, and Artificial Neural Networks. Lazy learners (instance-based learners) do not create any model immediately from the training data; they memorize the training data and search for the nearest neighbor from the whole training data each time a prediction is needed, making them very slow during prediction. Examples include K-Nearest Neighbor and Case-based reasoning. Eager learners are advantageous when fast prediction is needed after training, while lazy learners can be advantageous when the training data changes frequently or when quick training is desired at the expense of slow prediction.
